body.hook: Look around the room. Your chair, water bottle, phone case and backpack were all designed by someone who made choices about shape, material and colour. Good design is everywhere, and most of the time we don't even notice it, until something is badly designed.

study.title: Form Meets Function
study.question: How do designers balance how something looks with how it works?
study.passage:
Part 1, Object study (15 minutes): Each group gets three everyday objects (for example, a stapler, a reusable water bottle and a pair of scissors). For each object, answer:
• Function: What job does it do? Who is the user?
• Form: What shape, materials and colours were chosen?
• Ergonomics: How does it fit the hand or body?
• Aesthetic: Is it pleasing to look at? Why?
• Improvement: What would you change?
Part 2, Good vs bad design (10 minutes): Find one example of a frustrating design in the school (a door that you push when you should pull, a confusing sign, an uncomfortable chair). Explain why its form doesn't match its function.
Part 3, Sketch a redesign (20 minutes): Choose one object and draw three thumbnail sketches of an improved version. Label the changes and explain how each improves function or aesthetics.
Designers often say "form follows function": the shape should come from the job the object needs to do.

body.hook: You walk past buildings every day without noticing them, but architects planned every window, roof line and doorway. Alberta's buildings tell stories: grain elevators on the prairie, sandstone courthouses, glass towers in Calgary and Edmonton, and buildings designed to honour Indigenous ways of seeing the world.

study.title: Reading Buildings
study.question: How does architecture reflect place and purpose?
study.passage:
Alberta buildings to study (summaries written for this lesson; show images from public sources):
A. Prairie grain elevators: tall wooden towers built near railways from the early 1900s to store grain. Their height let gravity move grain into rail cars. Few remain, and some are now heritage sites.
B. Alberta Legislature Building, Edmonton (completed 1913): Beaux-Arts style with a large dome, columns and sandstone, designed to look important and permanent.
C. Canadian Museum of History, Gatineau (1989), designed by Douglas Cardinal, an Alberta-raised architect of Blackfoot and Métis heritage: flowing curved walls inspired by the land shaped by wind and water. Cardinal also designed St. Mary's Church in Red Deer (1968).
D. A modern glass office tower in downtown Calgary.
Task: For two buildings, sketch the facade, list materials, describe the form (tall, curved, symmetrical), and explain how the building suits its purpose, climate and community.

body.objective: Students will be able to critique a design.
successCriteria: I can critique a designed object using criteria
I can balance form, function and aesthetics in a judgement

body.hook: Some chairs are so uncomfortable that nobody sits in them, even though they look amazing. Some cheap water bottles leak the first week. Designers make choices, and a good critic can explain exactly which choices worked and which failed.

vocabulary.definition: A careful judgement of strengths and weaknesses using evidence.

study.title: Design Critique
study.question: How do I judge whether a design succeeds?
study.passage:
Design critique method (written for this lesson):
1. Describe: What is it? What is it made of? What are its parts?
2. Function: What job does it do? Test it if possible. Does it work well for the user? Is it comfortable (ergonomics)? Is it safe?
3. Aesthetics: What does it look like? Which elements of art (line, shape, colour, texture) are used? What mood or message does it give?
4. Judge: Does the form suit the function? Who is it designed for? Is it sustainable?
5. Improve: Sketch one redesign that fixes a weakness.
Objects to critique (bring in or use photos): a school chair, a reusable water bottle, a backpack, a pair of scissors, a phone case, a famous chair design such as the Eames Lounge Chair (1956).
